lessons.title: Lesson 1: Writing a SMART goal
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn a vague wish into a SMART goal.
This lesson builds toward: Given a vague wish, you will rewrite it as a SMART goal for the next four weeks, with every letter of SMART checked.
"Get in shape" or "find a job" are wishes. They are a good start, but they do not tell you what to do today. A SMART goal turns a wish into something you can act on and measure.
SMART stands for Specific (exactly what), Measurable (a number or a clear finish line), Achievable (stretching but possible), Relevant (it matters to you) and Time-bound (a deadline). "Find a job" becomes "Apply to 10 warehouse or kitchen jobs by 30 November." "Get faster" becomes "Cut 2 seconds off my 400-metre time by the end of the season."
Notice the job goal is about what you control (applying), not what you do not (being hired). Goals you control keep you moving even when others are slow to answer.
Step by step:
- Write your wish in a few words.
- Make it specific: what exactly?
- Add a number or a clear finish line.
- Check it is possible with the time and help you have.
- Check it matters to you.
- Add a deadline.
Words to know:
- SMART goal: a goal that is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.
- Deadline: the date by which something should be done.
Try it now: Write one wish you have right now. Then rewrite it as a SMART goal for the next four weeks. Check each letter: S, M, A, R, T.
You can now turn a vague wish into a SMART goal with a number and a deadline.

check.q: What does the M in SMART stand for?
check.why: Measurable means you can count or check whether you did it.

check.q: Your wish is "get in shape." What would you write instead?
options: "Jog 20 minutes, 3 days a week, for the next 4 weeks"
"Be the strongest person in the gym"
check.why: This goal is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Breaking a goal into weekly steps
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Break a SMART goal into weekly steps and a first small action.
This lesson builds toward: Starting from your SMART goal, you will break it into one step per week and a small next action, with a next action you can do in about 15 minutes.
A four-week goal can feel big. Breaking it into weekly steps makes it doable. Work backwards from the deadline: what needs to be true by the end of week 4, week 3, week 2 and week 1?
For "Apply to 10 jobs by 30 November": week 1, update the résumé and list 15 places; week 2, apply to 3; week 3, apply to 4; week 4, apply to 3 and follow up on all. For a small business goal of 5 new customers: week 1, list 30 people to contact; weeks 2 to 4, contact 10 a week.
Then pick the very next action, small enough to do in 15 minutes or less, such as "Open my résumé and fix the phone number." An AI assistant can suggest steps if you are stuck; ask it, then cut its list down to what fits your real week.
Step by step:
- Write the goal and deadline at the top.
- Work backwards: what must be done each week?
- Write one step per week.
- Write the next small action you can do in 15 minutes.
- Do that action today if you can.
Words to know:
- Milestone: a checkpoint on the way to a goal, such as the end of each week.
- Next action: the very next small, physical thing you will do.
Try it now: Take your SMART goal from Lesson 1. Write one step for each of the four weeks, then write the next small action and do it now if you can.
You can now break a goal into weekly steps and choose a small next action.

options: The final result of your goal
A small, physical step you can do in about 15 minutes
check.why: A next action is tiny and clear, so you can start right away.

check.q: An AI assistant gives you 25 steps for your goal. What would you do?
options: Try to do all 25 this week
Ask AI to make the goal for you
Trim it to steps that fit your real week
check.why: AI can suggest steps, but you trim them to fit your real time.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Planning your week
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan a week with time blocks for what matters most.
This lesson builds toward: For the coming week, you will plan your calendar with fixed things first, time blocks for your goal and a buffer block, with at least two goal blocks and one empty buffer.
A plan for the week turns goals into time on the calendar. Choose a set time, such as Sunday evening, and spend 15 minutes on it.
First, put in what is fixed: work shifts, classes, practices, appointments, parole or probation check-ins, family duties and sleep. Then add time blocks for your goal steps, such as "Tuesday 6-7 pm: apply to 2 jobs." Treat these blocks like appointments with yourself.
Leave some empty space. Things go wrong, buses run late and kids get sick. A plan with no room for surprises breaks on day one. Use whatever you will actually look at: a paper planner, a whiteboard, or a free calendar on your phone with reminders.
Step by step:
- Pick a weekly planning time (for example Sunday evening).
- Add the fixed things: work, school, practice, appointments, sleep.
- Add time blocks for this week's goal step.
- Leave some empty space for surprises.
- Set reminders for the most important blocks.
Words to know:
- Time block: a set piece of time on your calendar for one task.
- Buffer: spare time you leave empty for surprises.
Try it now: Plan next week on paper or a phone calendar. Put in the fixed things, then add at least two time blocks for your goal step and one empty buffer block.
You can now plan a week with fixed commitments, goal time blocks and buffer time.

options: Empty time left in your week for surprises
Time for your most important task
A block of time for sleep only
check.why: Buffer time gives your plan room when things go wrong.

check.q: You are planning next week. What would you put on the calendar first?
options: Fixed things like work, practice and appointments
Nothing; plan each day in the morning
check.why: Fixed things go in first, then goal blocks fit around them.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Choosing priorities
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Sort tasks by urgent and important and choose your top three.
This lesson builds toward: Given a to-do list of ten tasks, you will sort the tasks by urgent and important and choose your top three, circling the one you will do first.
There is always more to do than time allows. Priorities decide what gets your best time. One simple tool sorts tasks into four boxes using two questions: Is it important (does it move my goals or protect my health, family, job or freedom)? Is it urgent (does it need doing now)?
Important and urgent: do it now (a rent payment due today, a check-in appointment). Important, not urgent: schedule it (studying, training, building your business). Urgent, not important: keep it short or hand it off (many calls and messages). Neither: drop it (endless scrolling).
Most growth lives in the important but not urgent box, and it is the easiest to skip. Each morning or evening, pick your top three tasks for the next day and do the most important one first, before messages pull you away.
Step by step:
- List everything on your mind.
- Ask of each: is it important? Is it urgent?
- Put each task in one of four boxes: do now, schedule, keep short or hand off, drop.
- Pick your top three for tomorrow.
- Do the most important one first.
Words to know:
- Priority: something that matters more and gets done first.
- Urgent: needs doing soon.
- Important: moves your goals or protects what matters most.
Try it now: Write down ten things on your to-do list. Put each in one of the four boxes. Then choose your top three for tomorrow and circle the one you will do first.
You can now sort tasks by important and urgent and choose a top three for each day.

check.q: Which box does a check-in appointment due today go in?
check.why: It must be done today and it matters, so it is urgent and important.

check.q: Your phone keeps buzzing with group-chat messages while you work on a job application. What would you do?
options: Finish the application first and check messages later
Stop the application for the day
check.why: Most messages are urgent-feeling but less important than your top task.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Beating procrastination
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use simple tricks to start a task you have been putting off.
This lesson builds toward: Given a task you have been putting off, you will start it using a tiny first step, no distractions and a 10-minute timer, starting within the same session.
Procrastination is not laziness. We usually put things off because the task feels too big, unclear, boring or scary. The fix is to make starting easier.
Four tricks that work. Shrink it: make the first step tiny, such as "write one sentence of the cover letter." Use a timer: work for just 10 minutes; you can stop after, but often you keep going. Remove distractions: put the phone in another room or turn on do-not-disturb. Pair it: do the task at the same time and place each day, or with a study or workout partner.
Be kind to yourself when you slip. Blaming yourself makes the task feel worse. Notice it, pick the tiny first step, and start again.
Step by step:
- Name the task you are avoiding.
- Ask why: too big, unclear, boring or scary?
- Shrink it to a tiny first step.
- Set a timer for 10 minutes.
- Put your phone away and start.
- When the timer ends, choose: stop or keep going.
Words to know:
- Procrastination: putting off something you know you should do.
- Do not disturb: a phone setting that silences calls and alerts for a while.
Try it now: Pick one task you have been avoiding. Shrink it to a tiny first step, put your phone away, set a 10-minute timer and start right now.
You can now start a task you have been avoiding by shrinking it, timing it and removing distractions.

check.q: Why do people often put off a task?
options: It feels too big, unclear, boring or scary
They have too much free time
check.why: Tasks that feel big, unclear, boring or scary are the ones we avoid.

check.q: You have avoided cleaning out your garage for months. What would you do?
options: Plan to do it all next Saturday
Pick up one box, set a 10-minute timer and start now
check.why: A tiny first step and a timer make it easier to start.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Tracking progress and the weekly review
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Track your progress and adjust your plan in a five-minute weekly review.
This lesson builds toward: After seven days of tracking, you will complete a five-minute weekly review and change next week's plan, answering all three review questions and making at least one change.
What gets tracked gets done. A simple tracker shows you are moving, which keeps you going. It can be a list on paper with a tick for each day you did your step, a number in your phone notes (applications sent, money saved, miles run), or a free habit app.
Once a week, do a five-minute review. Ask three questions: What did I get done? What got in the way? What will I change next week? Then plan the next week using what you learned.
If you keep missing a step, the plan is the problem, not you. Make the step smaller, move the time, or change the deadline. Coaches change the training plan when an athlete is not progressing; do the same for yourself. Celebrate small wins too.
Step by step:
- Choose one number or tick to track each day.
- Record it at the same time each day.
- Once a week, ask: what got done, what got in the way, what will I change?
- Adjust next week's plan.
- Celebrate one small win.
Words to know:
- Tracker: a simple record of what you did each day.
- Weekly review: a short look back each week to learn and adjust your plan.
Try it now: Final task: track your goal step every day for seven days. On day 7, answer the three review questions in writing and plan the next week with at least one change.
You can now track progress on a goal and use a weekly review to adjust your plan.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds SMART goal The goal is vague or has no deadline or number. A four-week goal that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. The goal focuses on actions the learner controls. Weekly steps No weekly steps, or steps are too big to start. One step for each week and a small next action. Steps were planned backward from the deadline. Week plan No time blocks, or fixed things missing. Fixed things first, time blocks for the top three priorities, and one buffer block. The most important task is planned early in the day. Getting started and tracking Put off the steps, or fewer than seven days tracked. Seven days tracked, showing what was actually done. Notes which start tricks helped on hard days. Weekly review Review missing, or no change planned. Answers what got done, what got in the way, and what will change, with at least one change. The change is already placed on next week's calendar. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: How long should a weekly review take?
check.why: A short review is easy to keep doing every week.

check.q: Your tracking shows you never did your goal step on weekday mornings. What would you do?
options: Keep the same plan and hope
Move the step to a time that worked better
check.why: The review is for changing the plan when it is not working.
